items.title: UK charity shop profits plummet amid shift in secondhand clothes market
items.summary: British Heart Foundation describes ‘exceptionally challenging’ trading after Oxfam’s retail profit reportedly fell 23% amid rise of platforms such as Vinted Profits at some of the UK’s best-known charity shops have plummeted as they face a number of pressures, including from…
items.body: Profits at some of the UK’s best-known charity shops have plummeted as they face a number of pressures, including from online secondhand clothes platforms, prompting claims that a key part of the sector’s fundraising model could be under threat. According to unpublished accounts seen by the Financial Times , Oxfam’s retail profit fell 23% to £4.9m in the last financial year, compared with £6.4m in the previous year. The British Heart Foundation (BHF), which has the biggest high street presence of any charity in the country, has announced plans to close 150 stores after they made a £3.3m loss in the last financial year. Cancer Research UK and Scope have also closed, or are closing, some of their shops. But these losses come despite UK spending on secondhand clothing having quadrupled over the past decade, rising to £8.8bn a year, according to GlobalData.

items.title: How China’s ‘enchanting’ farms became a draw for foreign tourists
items.summary: When the travel agency China Highlights organises bus trips for foreign tourists to iconic sights across China, the company says one last-minute request keeps cropping up again and again. “Can we visit a farm?” The question has become so common that guides now organise farm…
items.body: When the travel agency China Highlights organises bus trips for foreign tourists to iconic sights across China, the company says one last-minute request keeps cropping up again and again. “Can we visit a farm?” The question has become so common that guides now organise farm tours lasting a day or two for groups as they drive back from scenic spots such as Huangshan and Zhangjiajie, according to company CEO Steven Zhao. The tourists often wanted to meet the farmers, have lunch in their single-storey brick homes and even join a harvest, he added. The trend is part of a wider shift in China’s tourism market, as travellers both domestic and foreign branch out from famous urban landmarks and mountain scenic areas. The change is partly being driven by the rise of selfie tourism.

items.title: Binance says 90% of $6.3 billion hack losses are now covered, plans to resume withdrawals Sunday

items.body: Binance said Saturday that it has covered up to 90% of the roughly $6.3 billion in token assets stolen from its hot wallets in a record crypto theft announced Thursday. Separately, the FBI said late Saturday that ​it has determined North ​Korea ​was responsible for the ⁠theft. Binance said it will continue to buy the remaining relevant token assets through market and over-the-counter channels until the covered amount reaches 100% for all tokens. "All BTC, ETH, USDT, BNB, SOL, USDC, XRP, USD1, RLUSD, and ZEC are fully backed 100%," Binance said in a statement .

items.title: Railway engineering work over Christmas will cause 10 days of disruption
items.summary: London Paddington and Birmingham New Street stations will shut for five days but most routes will stay open Passengers travelling on some of Great Britain’s busiest railway lines at Christmas have been warned of significant disruption from 10 days of engineering works. Work will…
items.body: Passengers travelling on some of Great Britain’s busiest railway lines at Christmas have been warned of significant disruption from 10 days of engineering works. Work will close London’s Paddington station – affecting intercity trains to the west of England and Wales until January – as well as Birmingham New Street, the UK’s busiest station outside the capital, for five days over the holiday period. Passengers travelling between London , north-east England and Scotland will have to negotiate the part closure of the east coast mainline on Christmas Eve. Direct trains from the capital to parts of Essex and Norfolk will also be cut for much of the festive period. Network Rail said most routes would still stay open and that the Christmas period, when train services generally stop for 25 and 26 December, remained the best time to conduct essential works.

items.title: Shenzhen too pricey? Cost-conscious Hongkongers dig deeper into mainland China
items.summary: Seventy-something Hong Kong retiree Leung Ching says a meal for four in Shenzhen, the megacity in mainland China roughly an hour’s train ride away, that cost just over 300 yuan (US$45) a few years ago now runs to 500 to 600 yuan. It would cost around HK$1,000 (US$127.50) in Hong…
items.body: Seventy-something Hong Kong retiree Leung Ching says a meal for four in Shenzhen, the megacity in mainland China roughly an hour’s train ride away, that cost just over 300 yuan (US$45) a few years ago now runs to 500 to 600 yuan. It would cost around HK$1,000 (US$127.50) in Hong Kong, but only 300 yuan in Guangzhou and just 200 yuan in Zhongshan, two cities within two hours of Hong Kong. “Shenzhen is becoming less and less affordable,” said Leung, a retired vendor. Last year, consumer prices in Shenzhen rose 0.2 per cent year on year, including a 0.2 per cent rise in food, tobacco and alcohol prices, a 1 per cent increase in clothing and a 2.8 per cent rise in healthcare, according to the city’s statistics bureau. Leung’s experience points to an emerging trend.

items.title: Qatari mediators held talks in Tehran aimed at restarting direct U.S.-Iran negotiations, source says
items.summary: Axios reported that Qatari mediators held more than 12 hours of talks in Tehran on Friday to reach a deal to avoid a resumption of American-led attacks on Iran.
items.body: Qatari mediators have held talks with Iranian officials in an attempt to restart direct negotiations between Washington and Tehran, an official source familiar with the discussions told CNBC on Saturday. Iran promised a "geographically unrestricted response" to any new attacks by the U.S. Qatari mediators held more than 12 hours of talks in Tehran on Friday to reach a deal to avoid a possible resumption of American-led attacks on Iran after the U.S. midterm elections, the source said, speaking on condition of anonymity. Axios first reported the talks, which it said are set to continue in the Qatari capital, Doha, on Saturday. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said there are no plans to meet U.S. officials , adding that an Iranian delegation has headed to Qatar for talks with mediators, Qatari media outlet Al Jazeera reported.

items.title: City of London chief tops UK Black Powerlist
items.summary: Ian Thomas, who heads the City of London Corporation, tops the Black Powerlist in its 21st year.
items.body: Ian Thomas, chief executive of the City of London Corporation, has been named the UK's most influential Black Briton in this year's Black Powerlist awards. The 57-year old is the first Black person to oversee the Square Mile's governing body in its more than 900-year history. The City of London Corporation is an administrative body with responsibility for London's central financial district, headed by its own Lord Mayor. Thomas tops the 2027 Black Powerlist, which recognises the most powerful people of African and Caribbean heritage in the UK. The award body said he was "a respected public-service leader with over 30 years' experience in local government". Other influential names in this year's top ten include entrepreneurs Emma Grede and Steven Bartlett, as well as actor and filmmaker Sir Idris Elba.

items.title: Eight in 10 homes in London’s poshest postcodes now sell below asking price, Coutts finds
items.summary: Sellers in areas such as Belgravia and Mayfair face hundreds of thousands of pounds in losses as property prices fall Eight out of 10 properties in London’s most exclusive neighbourhoods – such as Mayfair, Belgravia and Knightsbridge – now sell below asking price, according to…
items.body: Eight out of 10 properties in London’s most exclusive neighbourhoods – such as Mayfair, Belgravia and Knightsbridge – now sell below asking price, according to research by Coutts, which provides private banking services to wealthy clients. Property prices in “prime central London”, which covers the city’s most expensive postcodes, have dropped 5% in the third quarter of 2026, as the slowdown in the UK’s property market hits its wealthiest residents. It means some affluent people are facing hundreds of thousands, if not millions, of pounds in losses to the value of their homes, with properties selling at an average 10% discount to their asking price, Coutts found. Prices in the highest end of London’s property market are now 14% below their peak in 2014, having been hit hard by Brexit, the Covid pandemic, higher property taxes and a surge in borrowing costs.

items.title: Trump defamation suit against Murdoch, WSJ over Epstein letter dismissed with prejudice
items.summary: By dismissing the suit with prejudice, Trump can't file another amended version in district court. Trump's legal team said the president plans to appeal.
items.body: A federal judge on Saturday dismissed President Donald Trump's defamation lawsuit against media baron Rupert Murdoch and The Wall Street Journal over the newspaper's reporting on a purported 50th birthday letter to notorious sex offender Jeffrey Epstein . U.S. District Judge Darrin Gayles in Miami ruled that Trump again failed to plausibly allege that the newspaper and other defendants acted with actual malice when they published the story in July 2025. "Grasping at straws, the Amended Complaint attempts to manufacture flaws with the investigation," Gayles wrote in the 20-page ruling, which dismissed the lawsuit with prejudice. The judge said the Journal had conducted a "thoughtful and detailed investigation" and rejected Trump's argument that the newspaper should not have published the story after he denied writing the letter.

items.body: High street brands that boomed in the noughties before the squeeze of both sustainably minded consumers and the rise of ultra-cheap online labels are staging a comeback. This time, rather than focusing solely on trend-led affordable designs, the names familiar to any shopper are courting luxury fashion, A-list collaborations and enhanced services in an attempt to engage consumers. Think Gap’s new collection with Victoria Beckham. Or Marks & Spencer showcasing a covetable catwalk collection at London fashion week with celebrities including Joan Collins and assorted gen Z Gallaghers in attendance, then making it available to buy immediately, with half of the pieces under £50. Topshop relaunched last year and now has concessions in 30 John Lewis stores, as well as the luxury retailer Liberty.

items.title: Trump called out Big Oil profits. Here’s how much their refining earnings have surged since
items.summary: Trump criticized Big Oil for making “too much money,” but oil majors have since reported surging refining earnings as fuel supplies tightened.
items.body: President Donald Trump scolded Big Oil in August , saying ExxonMobil and Chevron were making "too much money based on a shortage," as profits surged in the wake of the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran. Corporate results published this week laid out the windfall oil majors are continuing to get from tight fuel supplies and elevated refining margins amid global conflict. Shell , BP , TotalEnergies and Exxon reported sharply higher margins in their refined-products businesses , a gauge of the amount they earn from processing crude oil into gasoline, diesel and jet fuel. Chevron does not report a comparable, standalone refining-margin figure, but it reported Friday that its downstream earnings more than quadrupled from a year earlier to $4.9 billion, with the company citing higher margins on refined-product sales.

items.title: The cursed cruise: how the dream of never-ending luxury at sea became a nightmare
items.summary: The MV Odyssey was billed as the ultimate escape from Donald Trump. Instead, the oil shock caused by his war has left passengers unceremoniously dumped in Cambodia The idea was a never-ending retirement at sea, a continuous voyage around the globe. The promise to the passengers…
items.body: The idea was a never-ending retirement at sea, a continuous voyage around the globe. The promise to the passengers of the MV Odyssey cruise ship – many approaching the autumn of their lives – was that on the open seas they could cut loose from the troubles of the world. But the world had other ideas. The end came in an announcement as stark as it was brief: they had seven hours to get off. They were going no further than Cambodia . The Odyssey, owned by Florida-based Villa Vie Residences, which had first set sail from Belfast, Northern Ireland, in October 2024, made an explicit offer: Donald Trump had been re-elected to the White House, and this was a way for those ill-disposed to the president to enjoy a four-year “skip forward”.

items.title: Trump promised to slash energy costs — but gasoline, diesel and jet fuel all soared instead
items.summary: President Donald Trump promised voters who were angry about inflation that he would slash gasoline prices below $2 a gallon in his first year in office.
items.body: President Donald Trump promised voters angry about inflation that he would slash gas prices below $2 a gallon within his first year in office. "My plan will cut energy prices in half or more than that within 12 months of taking office," Trump said in a speech to the New York Economic Club in September 2024 during his re-election campaign. "Energy was what caused our problem initially," he told voters. "Energy is going to bring us back. That means we're going down and getting gasoline below $2 a gallon." But when voters head to the ballot box on Tuesday energy prices will remain a headache. Gas and diesel prices are forecast to be the highest ever on an election day, according to Patrick De Haan, head of petroleum analysis at GasBuddy. Gas prices stood at a national average of $4.20 a gallon on Friday, nearly 40% above the same period last year.

items.title: How ‘sin bin’ for red light jumpers saves cyclists from being saddled with a fine
items.summary: Police scheme in City of London offers errant cyclists a choice – watch a roadside safety video or pay a £50 penalty When Aman cycled through a red light in the City of London this week, he was surprised when the police pulled him over. He was positively shocked when, instead of…
items.body: W hen Aman cycled through a red light in the City of London this week, he was surprised when the police pulled him over. He was positively shocked when, instead of giving him a fine, officers took him into a gazebo to watch a bike safety film. Aman was one of 30 cyclists caught in the first 20 minutes that morning, as part of a new scheme by City of London police to dissuade cyclists from running red lights. Many concerned pedestrians have celebrated the time-out zone and, perhaps more surprisingly, cyclists have too. The new pop-up scheme, called “stop, look, listen, change”, gives offending riders the chance to view an educational film about the dangers of red light jumping. Those caught by police who do not want to pay a £50 fine are taken to a “sin bin” by the roadside, where they watch testimonies from visually impaired road users.

items.title: Trump boosted half of US coal plants with taxpayer dollars and ‘free passes to pollute’, report says
items.summary: Environmental Defense Fund analysis shows administration handed out $950m and Clean Air Act exemptions It’s a good time to be a coal plant in the US. The Trump administration has given support to almost half of the nation’s coal plants, helping them to continue operating despite…
items.body: It’s a good time to be a coal plant in the US. The Trump administration has given support to almost half of the nation’s coal plants, helping them to continue operating despite economic and regulatory headwinds, according to a new analysis by the Environmental Defense Fund. The analysis, which looked at the 184 operating coal plants that are connected to the grid, found that 90 received support from the Trump administration through “cash handouts, free passes to pollute, and requirements to stay online past their retirement dates”. The administration provided $950m in taxpayer dollars to 24 coal plants and handed Clean Air Act exemptions from toxic pollution limits to 70 coal plants, according to the EDF analysis. “It’s extending the life of these coal plants,” said Surbhi Sarang, director and senior attorney at the Environmental Defense Fund.

items.title: How to start an art collection on any budget
items.summary: A guide to beginning an art collection, including how to research artists, what to buy, and where to connect, from galleries to fairs to auction houses.
items.body: The decision to invest in any collectibles market should start with curiosity and love, and buying art is no exception. While the rarest works of art in the world have sold for hundreds of millions of dollars, for most collectors, art is unlikely to match the returns offered by traditional investment markets. A recent analysis of 10-year annualized returns including data through 2024 showed that the stock market vastly outperformed art. True, it has been an incredibly strong bull market on a historical basis, but the performance from the art market over the same time period produced some of the worst 10-year returns in seven decades. As with any asset class experiencing a downturn, some experts see the recent weakness as a buying opportunity. The 2025 market did see some improvement, and 2026 has been an ever better year to date, with younger buyers showing up in a big way.

items.title: ‘The last fortress’: historic Athens cafe closes as countercultural area gentrifies
items.summary: Mouria coffeehouse unable to renew lease in Exarchia, known for leftwing solidarity, resistance and radicalism It has been the hangout of writers, artists, poets and politicians, doctors and lawyers, radicals and revolutionaries for as long as anyone can remember. And for 44…
items.body: I t has been the hangout of writers, artists, poets and politicians, doctors and lawyers, radicals and revolutionaries for as long as anyone can remember. And for 44 years, Christos Vanas, the proprietor of Mouria, has let them all in. Every day at 7am, the taciturn former waiter has been the first man to step inside the historic cafe in Exarchia, the heart of leftwing Athens . It is a ritual he has kept punctiliously, opening up the famous gathering place before he himself has had his first coffee. “Only Saturdays are different,” says his daughter Areti, drawing on a Karelia, the aromatic Greek cigarette that, like Mouria, has been around for more than a century. “By 5am, he is here serving tsipouro and other [alcoholic] spirits to warm up the stallholders of the street market outside.” But this weekend will be Vanas’s last.

items.title: Intel stock has worst day since 1970s, wiping about $12 billion off government's stake

items.body: Intel shares plummeted 29% on Friday, their worst day since the 1970s, after the chipmaker issued weaker-than-expected guidance due to a plant shutdown in Israel and ongoing softness in the PC market. It's a major setback for CEO Lip-Bu Tan, who was hired in March 2025, and has since been on a campaign to revive the company after it missed out on the early years of the artificial intelligence boom. Intel's plunge is also a big hit to the Trump administration, which led the U.S. government into taking a 10% stake in the company over a year ago. While it's still a profitable investment, the value of those holdings dropped by about $12 billion on Friday. Nvidia also took a big stake in Intel, and its stock dropped by about $6 billion in value.

items.title: Britain’s housing crisis won’t be fixed without a new tax landscape
items.summary: We need policies that stop treating property as a store of wealth and that allow people to move home cheaply John Healey’s critics on the right and left accused him of dodging the big questions in his first budget . The chancellor failed to announce reforms that might tackle…
items.body: J ohn Healey’s critics on the right and left accused him of dodging the big questions in his first budget . The chancellor failed to announce reforms that might tackle some of Britain’s chronic problems, they say. Healey’s scatter-gun budget, as the Resolution Foundation called it, was more about politics than economics, and unapologetically so. Housing was one area of policy that took up a considerable chunk of his speech. And yet the measures amounted to very little, if a test of his policy changes was to ask how different will the UK be at the next election. Or, as that date is only two and a half years away, 10 years from now. Housing is more than a single element of a complex economy. It is both its driving force and a disease eating its way through the body, from the inside out. More than 80% of global investment is in property and the vast majority of that is in residential.

items.title: A world-first focus on long-term outcomes could transform UK government – or create new spending fights
items.summary: Tucked away in John Healey’s budget is decision to ringfence preventative projects where future savings outweigh initial cost It merited the briefest of mentions in John Healey’s speech and just one paragraph in the 166-page budget document , but some believe it could…
items.body: It merited the briefest of mentions in John Healey’s speech and just one paragraph in the 166-page budget document , but some believe it could revolutionise not just public spending but the very process of government itself: a new focus on long-term outcomes. The idea in the broad sense is very simple. Any spending deemed to be “preventative” – that is, the initial outlay will be more than made up for by future savings – will from now on be ringfenced, meaning it cannot be raided for more immediate needs. This might sound uncontroversial, but it follows many years of long-term spending being pillaged to plug day-to-day gaps, particularly so during and after the austerity measures of the 2010 coalition government, which slashed numerous prevention-based services, not least the Sure Start programme for families with young children.

items.title: 'Bad time to troll': Binance co-founder Zhao asks Musk for support after hack

items.body: Changpeng Zhao, the cofounder and former CEO of Binance , asked Elon Musk not to "troll" the company on Friday and instead "show some support" after the SpaceX CEO appeared to mock the embattled cryptocurrency exchange in a series of social media posts. After learning the world's largest crypto exchange had been hit by a $6.3 billion hack late Thursday, Musk posted several emojis, ranging from laughing to grimacing, on X. In response, Zhao reminded the SpaceX and Tesla CEO of Binance's equity stake in Musk's businesses. Binance’s SpaceX stake, which stems from an earlier investment in what was then-Twitter, is worth more than $1 billion, Zhao said. "Elon, have a lot of respect for you, but bad time to troll. Please stop," Zhao wrote. "Our SPCX shares (from our $500m investment in your Twitter takeover) are worth more than a billion. Would appreciate if you show a little support.

items.body: Voters under 50 probably won’t remember the “ welfare queen ”. But she once embodied Republicans’ claim of the underlying reason for US societal decay: the poor are a bunch of fraudsters. Ronald Reagan introduced Linda Taylor to US voters at a rally during the Republican presidential primary season in 1976. A resident of Chicago’s South Side, Taylor had been arrested for welfare fraud. “She used 80 names, 30 addresses, five phone numbers to collect food stamps, social security, veteran’s benefits for four non-existing deceased veteran husbands,” Reagan said. “Her tax-free cash income alone has been running $150,000 a year.” Taylor may have committed crimes worse than social security fraud. But she wasn’t living on anything near $150,000. Josh Levin, author of The Queen: The Forgotten Life Behind an American Myth, points out that she was only ever charged with stealing $9,000.

items.title: AI is coming to construction sites. But does it make workers safer?
items.summary: AI is flagging hazards on construction sites, but researchers say evidence that the technology prevents injuries remains limited.
items.body: When Shelley Copsey was appointed by the Ontario Teachers' Pension Plan, one of the world's biggest infrastructure investors, her job was to find ways to use technology to solve problems across its portfolio. She quickly learned that there were persistent problems facing front-line workers. Four years later, Copsey is CEO of FYLD, a London-headquartered software company that uses artificial intelligence to support workers in construction, utilities and infrastructure. It comes as AI plays an increasingly important role in some of the most physically demanding jobs, from maintaining roads and railways to working on construction sites. According to Copsey, when fieldwork goes wrong, attention usually turns to budgets or cash flow. "We always go to the back office and we're like: oh, if we could help them forecast the job better, maybe this wouldn't be a problem," she told CNBC.

items.summary: Replacing government grants with revenue streams from taxation will not in itself reduce regional inequalities. But the political implications are radical Following Wednesday’s budget, the Treasury minister, Torsten Bell, was challenged by the BBC’s Evan Davis on whether its…
items.body: F ollowing Wednesday’s budget, the Treasury minister, Torsten Bell, was challenged by the BBC’s Evan Davis on whether its modest series of “breathing space” measures could truly be said to have ended “40 years of neoliberalism”. This line of questioning is becoming a familiar one. Andy Burnham’s ringing declaration of long-term intent is now being regularly deployed by commentators to suggest an emerging gulf between rhetoric and action. Mr Bell’s response was a good one. Recalling how “Margaret Thatcher in the 1980s hugely hollowed out local government [and] tried to emasculate our big cities”, he called the fiscal devolution roadmap unveiled in the budget a step change and a really big deal.From 2028, mayoral strategic authorities will for the first time receive a share of income tax receipts, and from next year they will be allocated 20% of business rates revenue.

items.title: How crypto hacking funds isolated North Korea’s nuclear programme
items.summary: Cryptocurrency theft is estimated to generate half of the country’s foreign currency income North Korea plays by its own rules. The isolated, secretive and autocratic country is largely cut off from the world’s economic system – but when it comes to generating foreign earnings…
items.body: North Korea plays by its own rules. The isolated, secretive and autocratic country is largely cut off from the world’s economic system – but when it comes to generating foreign earnings it relies on some of the world’s most sophisticated hacking. Experts, such as TRM Labs, quickly attributed the extraordinary $6.3bn (£4.7bn) Binance cryptocurrency theft to TraderTraitor, an elite North Korean hacking unit that has also been known as the Lazarus Group. Though the link may not be proven yet, the pattern of behaviour is familiar. North Korea has a history of cryptocurrency theft dating back to 2017, focusing on the sector’s relatively lax security controls as a way of stealing money and generating revenues for its military, including its nuclear weapons programme.

items.title: Relying on AI is rotting your brain. But here’s what you can do about it | Carly Dober
items.summary: Each new tech product is designed to make our lives easier and keep us mindlessly entertained. Switch off: embrace discomfort – and boredom Ever longed for your own personal assistant? In the ever quickening tech race, Meta has recently launched Muse, a new AI personal agent .…
items.body: E ver longed for your own personal assistant? In the ever quickening tech race, Meta has recently launched Muse, a new AI personal agent . Unlike traditional chatbots, this little AI tool will be able to fill out forms for you, organise calendars, pay bills and make reservations. Meta describes Muse as a personal agent “ built for everyone ”. The launch comes at a time when AI agents have been making headlines for hacking into government websites , public agencies and businesses. However, my immediate concern is a little closer to home. I work as a psychologist, and I’m often talking to clients about lifestyle habits that lead to short-term gain but incur long-term pain. Our brains have a beautiful way of preferring the path of least resistance, of doing what is easiest to preserve our resources.

items.title: This budget fails to live up to Andy Burnham’s grand rhetoric | Letters
items.summary: Caitlin Boswell of Tax Justice UK and others on what Aditya Chakrabortty described as a ‘Martin Lewis budget’ Aditya Chakrabortty was spot-on in his analysis of John Healey’s budget ( Burnham promised big change – where was it? Instead we got the Martin Lewis budget, 28 October…
items.body: Aditya Chakrabortty was spot-on in his analysis of John Healey’s budget ( Burnham promised big change – where was it? Instead we got the Martin Lewis budget, 28 October ). It was a drop in the ocean of what is needed to bring about the scale of change this country needs and, importantly, was promised by Andy Burnham. As the affordability crisis rages on, people may feel some relief at the small cost of living measures announced for households and businesses. But when we’ve been told we’ll get a wholesale reset and an end to neoliberalism, 4p off the price of gherkins and a temporary tiny bank tax isn’t going to cut it. So, what’s the solution? The government must fairly tax the vast fortunes of the richest people and corporations, left mostly untouched.

items.title: ‘Bunch of baloney’: calls grow for Cop summit reforms as countries on track to fail nature targets
items.summary: Cop17, focused on protecting nature and restoring ecosystems, concludes on Saturday with critics saying system allows ‘one idiot’ to stall progress Calls are growing for major reforms to UN biodiversity summits as countries fail to deliver on their promises to halt the…
items.body: Calls are growing for major reforms to UN biodiversity summits as countries fail to deliver on their promises to halt the destruction of the natural world, with governments likely on track to continue their record of never having met a target in the 34-year history of the convention. Two weeks of negotiations at biodiversity Cop17 in Yerevan, Armenia, concluded on Saturday morning with countries vowing to redouble their efforts to meet this decade’s targets, which include commitments to protect 30% of the planet for nature, restore nearly a third of Earth’s degraded ecosystems and reform $500bn (£410bn) of environmentally damaging subsidies . Agreed just four years ago by nearly every government on the planet, they aim to transform humanity’s relationship with nature . Despite progress in some areas, governments are way off track on meeting almost all of the targets.

items.title: Suspicious bets returning £149,000 for predicting Ballon d’Or under investigation
items.summary: Bets predicted exact top-five men’s finishing order Organiser France Football has contacted police A series of suspicious bets that correctly predicted the exact top-five finishing order of this year’s Ballon d’Or and generated almost $200,000 (£149,000) in winnings is being…
items.body: A series of suspicious bets that correctly predicted the exact top-five finishing order of this year’s Ballon d’Or and generated almost $200,000 (£149,000) in winnings is being investigated by the event’s organisers, France Football, who have also contacted the police. It has been alleged that 12 Polymarket accounts – an American cryptocurrency-based prediction market – placed the bets, with more than $264,000 wagered on the outcome before Monday’s ceremony. Their extraordinary accuracy has raised serious questions about a potential leak of confidential results before football’s most prestigious individual award. Harry Kane was crowned the winner at the ceremony at the London Palladium, finishing ahead of Kylian Mbappé, Lamine Yamal, Rodri and Lionel Messi. Remarkably, this was the exact order predicted by the group of accounts identified in French media outlet Upside’s investigation .

items.title: Canada and EU announce new alliance open to like-minded countries
items.summary: Alliance for the Future, unveiled at Montreal summit and open to other countries, conceived for world ‘shaken by new storms’ Canada and Europe have announced a new alliance of like-minded nations to serve as both a “protective canopy under which our citizens can thrive” and a…
items.body: Canada and Europe have announced a new alliance of like-minded nations to serve as both a “protective canopy under which our citizens can thrive” and a powerful hedge against the unpredictable nature of geopolitics, while welcoming other countries to join. Speaking to reporters on Friday from Montreal, the prime minister, Mark Carney, and the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen , called the new partnership the Alliance for the Future and said the “deepest possible partnership between Canada and the 27-member bloc had the potential to offer unprecedented stability and opportunity”. “Our societies have been shaken by new storms,” Carney told reporters, referring to the damaging effects of the climate emergency but also the “erosion of democratic norms” and “the weaponization of trade”.

items.title: Tech sell-off drives US markets down by nearly $1tn after subpar earnings reports
items.summary: Big tech stocks falter as investors question whether billions being poured into AI can generate returns quickly enough A sell-off of tech stocks that began earlier this month and gained steam with disappointing earnings from leading tech companies drove US markets down by…
items.body: A sell-off of tech stocks that began earlier this month and gained steam with disappointing earnings from leading tech companies drove US markets down by hundreds of billions of dollars Friday. In total, the decline has knocked nearly $1tn in value off the tech-heavy Nasdaq exchange in one week and erased about $2tn in a month. The S&P 500, the index of the 500 most valuable companies in the US, fell by more than 1% Friday, losing hundreds of billions of dollars in market value. It was on track to erase its gain for October, even though it set its all-time high during the same month. The weakness for technology stocks dragged the Nasdaq composite down even further, more than 3%, also erasing hundreds of billions in value. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell less.
